Descriptive Epidemiology, where disease distribution is described under Time, Place, and Person.

1) TIME DISTRIBUTION 

Time distribution is divided into:

A) Short-term trends

  • Sudden changes over days to weeks

Includes:

  • Outbreak
  • Epidemic

B) Periodic trends

These are trends that occur repeatedly at fixed intervals.

They include:

1. Seasonal trend

  • Disease occurrence increases in a particular season every year
  • Example: Influenza in winter, diarrheal diseases in summer/rainy season

2. Cyclic trend (Key for this MCQ)

  • Disease occurrence shows repeated peaks and falls every few years
  • Classically described as 5–7 years interval in exams

Therefore, diseases occurring every 5–7 years are called cyclic trends.

C) Long-term trends

Secular trend

  • Occurs over decades
  • Reflects long-term changes due to:
    • immunization
    • sanitation
    • health services
    • socioeconomic progress

Why 5–7 years interval specifically indicates Cyclic trend?

Because cyclic trends represent multi-year recurrence due to:

  • accumulation of susceptible individuals
  • changes in herd immunity
  • strain variation (especially viral infections)
  • vector density cycles (vector-borne diseases)

High-Yield Examples of Cyclic Trends 

Disease      Cyclic interval

Dengue      1–3 years

Measles      2–3 years

Rubella       6–9 years

Influenza     7–10 years

Hence, the most precise term for 5–7 year interval is Cyclic trend.

Distractor Rationale 

Option A: Secular trend

  • Secular trends are long-term trends
  • Occur over many years/decades
  • Not a 5–7 year phenomenon

Option B; Time trend

  • “Time trend” is a general umbrella term
  • Includes:
    • Short-term
    • Periodic (seasonal + cyclic)
    • Long-term (secular)

So it is not the specific answer.

Option C: Periodic trend

  • Periodic trend is a broad category
  • It includes:
    • Seasonal trend
    • Cyclic trend

Since the question gives a specific multi-year interval (5–7 yrs), the best answer is the more specific term: Cyclic trend.

  • Subcutaneous injections are usually given at a 45- to 90-degree angle. The angle is based on the number of subcutaneous tissues present. Generally, give shorter needles at a 90-degree angle and longer needles at a 45-degree angle.

Steps in AMTSL:

1)      Inj. uterotonic within 1 minute of delivery of baby or immediately after delivery of anterior shoulder of baby (most imp step)

2)      Delayed cord clamping (Clamping cord in 1-3 mins of delivery

3)      Delivery of placenta by Controlled Cord Traction (modified Brandt Andreus technique).

4)      Intermittent assessment of uterine tone (Earlier: uterine massage)

Note: Early cord clamping is not a part of AMTSL.

Early Cord Clamping

·         Early cord clamping is indicated in:

§  Birth asphyxia

§  Rh isoimmunization

§  Diabetic mother

·         The benefits of delayed cord clamping for up to 60 seconds is an increase in total body iron stores, expand blood volume and a decrease in anemia incidence in the neonate.

·         On the other hand, delayed cord clamping can lead to a higher hemoglobin concentration, which increases risks for hyperbilirubinemia and extended hospitalization for neonatal phototherapy. Delayed cord clamping can also hinder timely neonatal resuscitation.

·         According to AIIMS Protocols in Neonatology, in uncomplicated preterm birth, delayed cord clamping should be attempted. This is done for a minimum time of 60 seconds after delivery for preterm infants not requiring immediate resuscitation after birth. It states that DCC must be done even if the mother has an HIV infection. But as per the NACO guidelines, early cord clamping is advised.
